title: AI Took the Routine Coding, So Where Will the Next Senior Engineers Come From?
partialText:
Why design engineers and AI systems architects are in demand, why AI-written code rots without them, and how deliberate practice rebuilds judgment

The software job market has split in two. At the bottom, the work that used to define an entry-level engineer, turning a clear ticket into a form, an endpoint, or a list page, is shrinking. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab track the shift through payroll records from ADP, the largest payroll processor in the United States. In the August 2026 revision of their paper Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, young workers in the jobs most exposed to AI have fallen well behind. Between late 2022 and mid-2026, employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in those jobs fell about 11 percent, while employment of the same age group in the least-exposed jobs grew about 10 percent. Workers aged 35 to 49 in the most exposed jobs grew about 10 percent as well. For software developers specifically, the 2026 AI Index from Stanford HAI, the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, reports that employment among those aged 22 to 25 has fallen nearly 20 percent since 2024. The Canaries authors do not claim AI is the only cause. In a February 2026 follow-up they wrote that it is not the sole driver, though interest rates fail to explain why entry-level hiring fell hardest where AI exposure is highest.

At the same time, two roles keep showing up in job postings and team reorganizations. The design engineer owns the place where software meets people. The AI systems architect owns the place where software meets models. Neither job is mainly about typing code. Both are about making decisions a model cannot make on its own, and getting them right under real constraints. Between them sits a growing middle of product code that AI writes faster than anyone can read.

Senior engineers are trusted with big decisions because of their judgment, and judgment has always come from small, routine work: writing the sorting algorithm in school, building the tenth form, debugging the hundredth off-by-one error. If AI now does that routine work, where will the next generation of senior engineers get theirs?

The answer this article defends is simple to state and harder to live:

Routine work used to build judgment as a side effect of the job. Now judgment has to be built through deliberate practice.

Why These Two Roles, and Why Now

Fred Brooks — the IBM manager who led the System/360 operating system project and wrote The Mythical Man-Month — split the difficulty of software into two kinds in his 1986 essay No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering, reprinted in IEEE Computer the following year. Accidental complexity comes from the tools: syntax, boilerplate, wiring one library to another. Essential complexity comes from the problem: what the system must do, how its parts interact, and what happens when the world does not cooperate.

Coding assistants are the strongest attack on accidental complexity ever built. They are excellent at producing the fortieth variation of a familiar component or endpoint. Even on business plans, with agent usage billed on top, they cost a company a small fraction of a junior engineer’s salary.

What they do not remove is the essence, and the essence tends to pile up at two edges of a product. One edge faces people: how an interface behaves for a tired user on a slow phone, a keyboard-only user, or a screen reader user. The other edge faces models: what data reaches them, what they are allowed to do, how their answers are checked, and what each answer costs. The code in the middle is increasingly generated. The decisions at the edges are not.

Figure 1 lays a product out from left to right, with people on one side, models and data on the other, and product code in between. Under each role sit the four decisions it owns. Those eight decisions are the subject of the next two sections.

That is why these two roles are growing while the generic implementer role is not. Companies still pay for code, but less and less for the typing. They pay for someone who owns how the product behaves at its edges, where it meets real people and real models.

The Design Engineer

For most of the last decade, design and frontend development were separated by a handoff. A designer produced mockups in Figma. A developer rebuilt them in code, guessing at every state the mockup did not show: loading, empty, error, too much text, too little screen. The product that shipped was a lossy copy of the one that was designed.

The design engineer removes the handoff. The role combines a designer’s taste and user research with real frontend engineering, and it ships the interface directly. AI tools make the role practical, because the scaffolding is cheap now. A design engineer can try four versions of an onboarding flow against real data in an afternoon and keep the one users actually finish.

But speed is the visible part. The valuable part is knowing what the generated code got wrong, and generated interfaces are wrong in predictable ways.

Ask a model for a searchable dropdown and it will produce one that looks right in a screenshot. Whether it works is another matter. The W3C — the World Wide Web Consortium, which publishes web standards — documents the correct behavior in its ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and the combobox pattern alone covers which element holds focus, how arrow keys move through options, what a screen reader announces, and how the list closes. Generated components routinely miss parts of it, because the web they learned from misses it too. WebAIM, a nonprofit accessibility organization at Utah State University, scans the home pages of the top one million websites every year, and in its 2026 report 95.9 percent failed automated checks against WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.

Performance fails the same way. Google measures real-world page experience with Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint for loading, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift for visual stability. A generated list that renders ten thousand rows at once, or an image whose size the page does not declare in advance, so the text jumps down the moment the image arrives, looks fine in a demo on a fast laptop and becomes slow and jumpy on the ordinary, inexpensive phones many users carry.

Table 1 pairs five everyday interface decisions with the version a model tends to produce and the check a design engineer runs on it. In every row, the generated version handles the case the prompt described, and the check covers the cases nobody typed into the prompt: the keyboard user, the account with ten thousand records, the request that times out halfway. None of these checks is hard to run. Every one of them, though, requires knowing what good looks like before the model produces anything.

The AI Systems Architect

The second role sits at the other edge. Once a company puts language models into its product, someone has to decide how data reaches the model, what the model may touch, how its answers are checked, and what it all costs per request. The AI systems architect owns those decisions.

A typical first project is a support assistant that answers questions from company documents. The demo takes a day. The real system takes months, because almost every component hides a decision with a failure attached.

Retrieval decides which documents the model sees. Chunk the documents too small and answers lose context; too large and the relevant sentence drowns. Retrieve too few passages and the answer is incomplete; too many and latency and cost climb. Permissions decide whose documents those are. A retrieval index that ignores access rights will cheerfully quote one customer’s contract to another customer.

Then there is prompt injection, the attack in which instructions hidden inside a document or web page hijack the model. OWASP — the Open Worldwide Application Security Project — ranks it first in its Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications. Simon Willison, the independent developer and co-creator of the Django web framework, named the dangerous combination in a June 2025 post the lethal trifecta: an AI agent that can read private data, can read untrusted content, and can send data out. Any agent with all three can be tricked into leaking what it knows.

This has already happened. In April 2026, Capsule Security, a startup that secures AI agents at runtime, disclosed a flaw it called ShareLeak in Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft’s tool for building business agents, tracked as CVE-2026–21520. As VentureBeat reported, an attacker submitted fake system instructions through a public comment field on a SharePoint form. The agent reading that form pulled customer records from connected SharePoint lists and emailed them to the attacker through Outlook. Microsoft’s safety checks flagged the request, and the data left anyway, because sending email was an action the agent was allowed to take. All three legs were there: untrusted text from the public, private customer data, and a way to send it out. The architect’s job is to make sure no single path holds all three. OWASP had already published a separate Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025, written for exactly this class of system.

The remaining decisions are less dramatic and just as expensive to get wrong. Evaluation means keeping a suite of real questions with known good answers and rerunning it before every change to a prompt, model, or retrieval setting; without it, every change is a guess. Cost means knowing what one answer costs and deciding where caching or a smaller model is good enough. Change management means planning for the day a provider updates or retires a model and the assistant’s behavior shifts with no code change at all.

Figure 2 follows one customer question through the assistant. The two most serious risks, data leaking across customers and prompt injection, attach to the permission check and the document search, before the model even runs. Cost and behavior changes attach to the model and the answer check. Beneath the pipeline sits the evaluation suite, the only control that touches every stage.

Very little of this involves writing algorithms from scratch. Nearly all of it concerns how parts fit together and how they fail. It is Brooks’s essential complexity with a new job title.

What If the Middle Rots?

Figure 1 makes the middle look settled: product code, increasingly written by AI, sitting quietly between the two roles that matter. That picture hides a problem. The middle is where AI writes the most code, and code written quickly by many hands, human or not, tends to decay.

None of this is new. In 1980, Meir Lehman — the computer scientist who studied how IBM’s OS/360 changed over its lifetime — published Programs, Life Cycles, and Laws of Software Evolution, and one of his laws states that a program’s complexity grows as it changes unless someone does work to reduce it. Ward Cunningham — the programmer who invented the wiki — gave the cost a name in his 1992 OOPSLA experience report: technical debt. AI repeals neither law. It changes the rate at which the debt accrues.

The decay follows a few predictable paths. The first is duplication. A model asked for a feature usually writes a fresh helper instead of finding the one that already exists three folders away. GitClear, a company that analyzes changes across large numbers of code repositories, published a 2026 maintainability study covering 623 million code changes. It reports that moved code, the usual signature of refactoring, fell from 21 percent of changed lines in 2022 to 3.8 percent in the first part of 2026, while copy-pasted lines rose from 9.4 to 15.7 percent. Developers are now about five times as likely to paste code as to refactor it.

The second path is inconsistency. Different prompts and different model versions solve the same problem in different ways, so a codebase ends up with three ways to fetch data and two styles of error handling. The third is tests that agree with the code instead of the requirement. When the same model writes both, the tests often encode the same misunderstanding as the code, and they pass.

Team-level data adds a warning. DORA, Google Cloud’s DevOps Research and Assessment program, found in its 2025 report that AI adoption is now linked to faster software delivery, but checking that the software actually works before it reaches users remains the unsolved challenge. It also described AI as “a mirror and a multiplier”: in cohesive organizations it boosts efficiency, and in fragmented ones it highlights weaknesses. A rotting middle is exactly the kind of weakness it multiplies.

The most serious risk is code that nobody can explain. In 1985 the Danish computer scientist Peter Naur argued in Programming as Theory Building that a program’s real substance is not its source code but the theory in its programmers’ heads: why each part exists and how it would change if the world changed. When the people holding that theory leave, the program starts to die even though every line remains. Generated code raises an uncomfortable possibility. Some of it never had a theory in anyone’s head to begin with.

The rot rarely shows up in the middle first. It surfaces at the edges. The design engineer sees pages that grow slower with every release and loading states that behave differently on every screen. The AI systems architect sees a new code path that skips the permission check, or a cost spike from a retry loop nobody remembers adding. Both roles depend on the middle, so neither can treat it as someone else’s problem.

Sometimes the failure surfaces very far from its cause. Cloudflare, the content delivery and security network, had exactly that kind of failure in its November 18, 2025 outage. A routine permissions change in a database made a query return duplicate rows, which roughly doubled the size of a feature file generated for Cloudflare’s bot detection system. The proxy code that loaded the file had a hard limit of 200 features, against about 60 in normal use. When the doubled file crossed the limit, the code panicked, and much of the network returned errors for about three hours. No AI was involved, and that is the point. This is how a middle fails: an old, unstated assumption meets a change made somewhere else. Generated code adds more of those assumptions, faster, and leaves fewer people who remember them.

The defenses are mostly old engineering discipline, applied on purpose:

  • Tests written from the requirement, not from the code, so the code and its tests do not share one misunderstanding. A model can draft them in a separate session that sees only the specification, and each test is then checked against what the requirement means.
  • Automated architecture checks. Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, and Patrick Kua call these fitness functions in Building Evolutionary Architectures (2017): tests that check the system’s structure rather than its behavior, run in the build, such as “every data access goes through the permission layer,” “the interface layer never imports the database,” or “the main bundle stays under a size budget.” They turn architecture decisions into checks an AI agent cannot quietly ignore.
  • A named owner for every module, someone who can explain why it works the way it does. This is Naur’s theory, assigned to a person.
  • A standing refactoring budget, a fixed share of each cycle spent consolidating duplicates and deleting dead code, rather than waiting for a rewrite.
  • Recorded agent instructions. The conventions file an AI coding agent reads, and the model version it runs on, belong in the repository and in code review like any other part of the build.

Figure 3 sets common decay paths against some of the guardrails that slow them. Tests written from the requirement catch tests that share the code’s mistakes. Architecture checks keep AI from multiplying the system’s weak spots, because every change has to pass the same structural rules. A named owner answers code nobody can explain. A refactoring budget pays down duplication. Recorded agent instructions prevent mixed patterns by keeping each new model version writing code the same way as the last.

The Hard Question: Can Judgment Exist Without the Routine Work?

Here is the objection, stated as plainly as possible. Both roles depend on judgment: knowing that ten thousand rows will freeze a phone, sensing that a retrieval setting will blow the latency budget, recognizing an injection risk before it ships. Judgment like that has always come from routine work. If an engineer never writes a sorting algorithm, never hand-builds a dropdown, never debugs a slow query at two in the morning, how does that engineer become someone who can be trusted with the big decisions?

The objection is right that judgment comes from practice. It is wrong to assume that practice can only come from routine work.

Big decisions are pattern recognition

Research on expertise is consistent on this point. In 1973, William Chase and Herbert Simon showed in Perception in Chess that chess masters could reconstruct a position from a real game after a five-second glance far better than novices could, yet lost most of that advantage when the pieces were placed at random. The masters were not smarter. They had stored tens of thousands of meaningful patterns, which the authors called chunks, from years of play. Gary Klein found the same thing in firefighters and military commanders in Sources of Power (1998; 20th anniversary edition, 2017): experienced decision-makers rarely compare options. They recognize the situation as one they have seen before and act on that recognition.

Architecture works the same way. A senior engineer who says “this design will fall over at scale” is usually not running a calculation. The design matches a pattern stored from earlier failures. The patterns are built from small, concrete experiences, and the routine work was where most engineers collected them.

The sorting algorithm was never the point

Nobody has needed to write a sorting algorithm in production for decades; every language ships one. Universities taught it anyway, because writing it built something the library could not: a felt sense of why n log n beats n squared, what an invariant is, and how a loop goes wrong at its edges.

That felt sense is still in demand, just in different places. Cloudflare offers a second lesson from six years before its 2025 outage. On July 2, 2019, a single regular expression in a firewall rule triggered catastrophic backtracking and pinned CPUs across its network, taking much of it offline. Cloudflare’s public postmortem reads like an algorithms lecture. No engineer at Cloudflare was paid to write a regex engine. The outage still came down to complexity intuition that is built by writing and breaking small algorithms.

The same intuition separates good decisions in both roles. A design engineer deciding whether to sort fifty thousand rows in the browser or ask the server for one page at a time is doing complexity analysis on a phone’s CPU budget. An AI systems architect deciding how many passages to retrieve is trading recall against latency and cost. Neither will ever write the underlying algorithm. Both still need a feel for how an approach will scale, and that feel comes from having written algorithms like it by hand.

What changed is where the practice comes from

So the routine work mattered, but not as output. It mattered as repetitions. Before AI, an engineer collected those repetitions without trying, because the job consisted of them. Now the job hands them to a model, and an engineer who wants the judgment has to collect them on purpose.

That shift has a cost the old arrangement hid. The routine work was paid practice: a junior engineer learned on company time, on tickets the company needed done anyway. Practice an engineer finds alone is usually unpaid, fitted into evenings and weekends, and it favors people who have those hours to spare.

Employers have a reason to hesitate. Engineers change jobs, and a company that trains a junior may watch that engineer leave for a competitor that trained no one. But if every company waits for someone else to do the training, the pool of seniors shrinks for all of them while the volume of generated code keeps growing. A junior role can be redesigned rather than deleted: new engineers can own evaluation suites, write tests from requirements, run the accessibility and prompt injection checks, and review AI pull requests alongside a senior. That work is useful from the first week, so it pays for itself even if the engineer later leaves.

This is what K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues called deliberate practice in their 1993 paper The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance: practice aimed at a specific weakness, with immediate feedback, done at the edge of current ability. It is less pleasant than ordinary work. It is also far more efficient, which is the good news hidden in the problem. An engineer who practices deliberately for a few hours a week can build patterns faster than one who absorbed them slowly through years of tickets.

Five drills that replace the routine work

Write it once by hand. The first time an engineer meets a concept that matters to the role, the engineer builds a small version without AI. For a design engineer: a debounced search box, a virtualized list, an accessible dialog with a focus trap. For an AI systems architect: a retrieval pipeline over a hundred documents, a retry with exponential backoff, a ten-question evaluation script. One honest build is enough. After that, generating it is fine, because the engineer can now tell when the generated version is wrong.

Predict, then generate. Before asking a model for a solution, the engineer writes down the expected approach, its complexity, and where it will probably break, then compares that guess with what the model produces. Psychologists Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf named the underlying effect, the generation effect, in their 1978 paper The Generation Effect: Delineation of a Phenomenon: people remember information they generate themselves far better than information they only read. Predicting first turns the model from an answer machine into a sparring partner.

Review like a senior. The habit is to read more code than one writes, and to read AI output as if it were a pull request from a capable but careless colleague. This matters more than it sounds. In Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (ACM CCS, 2023), Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, and Dan Boneh at Stanford found that participants with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more confident that it was secure. Skeptical review is the drill that corrects that confidence.

Break it on purpose. A design engineer throttles the network to a slow 3G profile and uses the interface, unplugs the mouse and works by keyboard alone, and turns on a screen reader. An AI systems architect feeds the assistant a document with hidden instructions to see whether it obeys them, and load-tests a toy service until it falls over to learn what fails first. Each failure seen in a sandbox is one fewer seen in production.

Write the decision down. Michael Nygard proposed architecture decision records in his 2011 post Documenting Architecture Decisions: short documents that capture a decision, its context, and its expected consequences. The drill is to write one for every meaningful choice, even small ones, and reread it six months later. Judgment needs feedback, and most engineers never find out whether their decisions were right because nobody wrote down what they expected. Public postmortems from companies such as Cloudflare offer the same feedback for decisions an engineer did not have to make personally, at no cost.

Figure 4 shows why the five drills can replace the routine tickets that engineers used to learn from. Before AI, routine tickets and the code review that followed built the pattern library in an engineer’s head. Now the drills build the same library, and that library is what big decisions draw on. The difference is that the tickets came with the job, while the drills happen only when an engineer goes looking for chances to practice.

How the Two Roles Are Interviewed

Interviews have adjusted to the same reality. If a model can produce a correct answer to a standard problem in seconds, a candidate who produces the same answer silently has shown very little. Some companies have responded by allowing AI in their interviews. In June 2025, Canva — the Australian online design platform — published a post on its engineering blog telling engineering candidates it expected them to use AI coding tools during technical interviews. It redesigned its questions to be more complex, ambiguous, and realistic to match. Weeks later, 404 Media — the independent technology news site — reported that Meta would let some coding candidates use an AI assistant, because in the company’s own words that setup is “more representative of the developer environment that our future employees will work in.”

The structure that tests judgment best is a funnel: a broad prompt that a model could also answer, then constraints that break the first answer, then trade-offs and failure modes that only real understanding can handle. The two roles get different funnels.

Figure 5 sets them side by side. Both have the same shape, a broad prompt, then added constraints, then trade-offs and failure, but the constraints differ because the two roles guard different edges.

A design engineer candidate might be asked to build a searchable dropdown with AI assistance allowed. The first version will look fine. Then the interviewer unplugs the mouse, turns on a screen reader, loads ten thousand options, and throttles the device. At the narrow end come the real questions: virtualize or paginate, and why? What did the AI get wrong in the first version? A candidate who answers “it rendered every option and forgot to announce the active one” has shown exactly the skill the role pays for.

An AI systems architect candidate might be asked to design a support assistant over company documents. The first sketch, a vector database and a model call, is what any tutorial produces. Then the constraints arrive: some documents are customer contracts, one document contains hidden instructions, and each answer must cost less than a set budget. The narrow end asks what fails first under load, and how the team would know if a provider’s model update quietly made answers worse. In both funnels, the interviewer is really checking whether the practice happened.

Paths Into Each Role

Neither role requires starting over. Both grow out of work many engineers already do.

Table 2 maps common starting points to the role each leads toward, what to add, and a first project that proves the move. The last row matters most, because new graduates are where the next senior engineers have to come from. A new graduate will not start in either role as a senior, but a graduate who can show a small project with honest decision records, a working evaluation suite, or a fully accessible component already has evidence of judgment.

Conclusion

The worry about where the next senior engineers will come from is reasonable. If AI writes the routine code, the path to expertise looks paved over. It is not. The path was always the repetitions, not the code, and the repetitions are still available to any engineer willing to seek them out and any company willing to build them into junior roles.

The design engineer and the AI systems architect are growing because they own the decisions a model cannot own: how software treats people and how software treats models. The middle between them still needs people who can read it, or it will rot faster than any team can notice. The next senior engineers will come from the ones who kept practicing the small work deliberately, long after the job stopped requiring it.

AI took the routine work, and the practice that came with it. The engineers who replace it with deliberate practice will be the ones trusted with the big decisions.

Thanks for reading.

title: AG-UI Explained — How AI Agents Talk to Front-End and Where It Fits with MCP and A2A
partialText:
Why this protocol exists, what actually goes over the wire, what to watch out when you are building with it.

Imagine this scenario for yourself — you open an assistant inside your company’s expense tool and type: “File my expenses for last week’s trip”. You press enter, and you see progress in the form of a spinner. The spinner keeps running for x seconds, then x+n seconds, and so on, and finally you get an answer. “Done. Your report is submitted”.

Now ask a question to yourself — Did it help you understand what went behind the scenes? Like a taxi ride reported twice, or maybe dinner expenses were spent over the limit. Was it able to read all the receipts, or skipped a couple. The work was done, and you got a one-line message of completion without any evidence of what happened beneath.

If you have been building AI agents, I am sure you might have experienced this, because this is how agents are designed to work. An Agent does lot of things behind the scenes between the question you asked and answer that was synthesized, but by default not all steps are visible to the users. AG-UI protocol tries to fills exactly this gap.

I will try to explain this in way that I would to a newly joined developer in my team. We’ll start with the problem first, then look at why a shared protocol is the right fix, then read the actual messages that go over the wire, then cover where things break, and finally how AG-UI relates to MCP and A2A, which you have probably heard of. I’ll use a single example thoughout so that every idea lands on something concrete.

The example we’ll follow

We will start with the same expense agent and try to understand what it does behind the scenes in the x+n seconds that it takes:

  1. It reads twelve receipts from your trip.
  2. It asks the expense system what has already been filed.
  3. It notices two receipts for the same taxi ride and drops one, leaving eleven.
  4. It notices one dinner is over the company’s $x limit and needs a human decision.
  5. It submits the expenses.

Everything useful happened in the middle, and you were able to see none of it.

What’s actually wrong with only showing the spinner

From user experience standpoint, the problem perceived is only around the long wait times. It’s really frustrating to have to wait for so long to see an answer, but not be able to see where the time actually was spent. There are two problems that need attention:

First is trust — every answer generated should leave a trace, that helps validate the response. Let‘s say if you submitted an expense twice the agent should report it instead of silently removing it.

Second is control — There could be situations where agent might want a second opinion e.g. in case of dinner charges over the limit might have already been approved by manager, but agent refused. If the agent is silent, it would guess the input, which the finance team would assume it was wrongly submitted.

This isn’t as obvious as just streaming text

Anyone’s first instinct might be to conclude this is any easy problem to solve, because LLMs are capable of streaming tokens, so pipeing the response to UI should be a straight task.

This only covers about a third of what is needed. A proper agent screen would have three separate jobs:

Showing progress — Not only the words the agent is typing, but what it is doing: which tool it is calling, with what input, and what came back.

Sharing data — The expense list on screen should match the expense list the agent is working with, at every moment. If the agent marks the taxi as a duplicate, the row on screen should change right then, without a page reload and without the screen asking.

Handing control to a human — When the agent reaches a decision it shouldn’t make alone, it needs a way to stop, ask, and continue with your answer.

Now let’s think about the fact who has to build these three things. Every agent framework has its own idea of what “progress” looks like for e.g LangGraph exposes its graph state one way, CrewAI reports task output another way, and a hand-written agent loop does whatever its author felt like that day. Every frontend, in turn, wants its own shape of data. Hence lets say if you have N agent frameworks and M frontends, you end up writing something close to N × M custom integrations.

This is the problem AG-UI tries to solve. The team behind CopilotKit kept hitting it while building integrations with frameworks such as LangGraph and CrewAI and they solved the same streaming and state-sync problems over and over, and eventually pulled the common pattern out into a standalone protocol that any agent and any frontend can speak. The name stands for Agent-User Interaction protocol, and it is open source under the MIT license.

Lets understand AG-UI, in plain terms

AG-UI is a list of small, labeled messages, which it calls events. The agent sends them while it works, and our app listens and updates the screen. The agent says what just happened, in an agreed format, and the app doesn’t need to know which framework produced it.

The exchange has two halves —

  • Our app sends one HTTP request with the user’s message and a description of the current screen.
  • The agent answers with a stream of events — the most common way to carry that stream is Server-Sent Events (SSE), which is a long-lived HTTP response where the server keeps pushing lines of text. WebSockets and webhooks also works, because the AG-UI protocol cares only about the shape of the messages e.g. a JSON object with "type": "TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT" and a delta, and not how they travel.

Here is the request for our example

{
  "threadId": "thread_42",
  "runId": "run_7",
  "messages": [
    { "id": "m1", "role": "user", "content": "File my expenses from last week's trip." }
  ],
  "state": {
    "expenses": [
      { "id": 1, "vendor": "Metro Air",     "amount": 412.50, "status": "pending" },
      { "id": 2, "vendor": "Hotel Aurora",  "amount": 280.00, "status": "pending" },
      { "id": 3, "vendor": "City Cabs",     "amount": 38.00,  "status": "pending" },
      { "id": 4, "vendor": "City Cabs",     "amount": 38.00,  "status": "pending" },
      { "id": 5, "vendor": "Harbour Grill", "amount": 310.00, "status": "pending" }
    ]
  },
  "tools": [],
  "context": [],
  "forwardedProps": {}
}

Each field has a job:

  • threadId identifies the whole conversation, and runId identifies this one execution of the agent inside it. One thread can have many runs.
  • messages is the conversation so far.
  • state is what the screen currently knows. Notice that the app sends its own state to the agent, so both sides start from the same picture. (I've shown five of the twelve receipts to keep it readable.)
  • tools lists any functions the frontend itself can run on the agent's behalf.
  • context carries extra background information, and forwardedProps is a pass-through for anything cust om.

The agent’s response is the interesting part, so let’s read it slowly —

One run, event by event

Over SSE, each event arrives as a data: line holding a JSON object, followed by a blank line. On the wire it looks like this:

data: {"type":"RUN_STARTED","threadId":"thread_42","runId":"run_7"}

data: {"type":"TEXT_MESSAGE_START","messageId":"msg_1","role":"assistant"}

data: {"type":"TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT","messageId":"msg_1","delta":"Reading your receipts"}

I’ll drop the data: prefix from here on and describe what the screen does at each point. The payloads below are simplified slightly, so check exact field names against the current spec before you copy them into production code.

1. The run starts

{ "type": "RUN_STARTED", "threadId": "thread_42", "runId": "run_7" }

This is the first event of every run — It tells our app “the agent has started working”, so the app knows a run exists before any text or tool call arrives. On screen: a “working” indicator appears, and the send button turns into a stop button. The app also saves the runId, so it can match later events to this run.

Every run has a matching last event: RUN_FINISHED when it succeeds, or RUN_ERROR when it fails. Together they mark where the run begins and ends, and everything the agent does happens between them. Because a run always ends with one of the two, the UI would always knows when to remove the working indicator, even if something went wrong.

2. The agent starts talking

{ "type": "TEXT_MESSAGE_START",   "messageId": "msg_1", "role": "assistant" }
{ "type": "TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT", "messageId": "msg_1", "delta": "Reading your " }
{ "type": "TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT", "messageId": "msg_1", "delta": "receipts now." }
{ "type": "TEXT_MESSAGE_END",     "messageId": "msg_1" }

On screen, an empty chat bubble appears as soon as the message starts. The words fill in as each chunk arrives, and when TEXT_MESSAGE_END comes, the typing cursor disappears.

You might ask why one message takes three events instead of a single event carrying the whole sentence. Lets image a single-event version — The screen stays blank until the agent has finished writing, then the entire message appears at once. That’s the same pinner problem that we mentioned at the start of the write-up, just on a smaller scale.

Splitting the message into START, CONTENT and END gives our UI three clear moments to react to:

  • START: a new message exists, so show an empty bubble.
  • CONTENT: here’s the next piece, so add it to the bubble.
  • END: the message is complete, so stop the typing cursor.

The messageId ties all the pieces of one message together. That matters because an agent can have more than one message in progress at the same time, and the ID keeps their text from getting mixed up.

3. The agent calls a tool

{ "type": "TOOL_CALL_START",  "toolCallId": "call_1", "toolCallName": "check_existing_expenses", "parentMessageId": "msg_1" }
{ "type": "TOOL_CALL_ARGS",   "toolCallId": "call_1", "delta": "{\"week\":" }
{ "type": "TOOL_CALL_ARGS",   "toolCallId": "call_1", "delta": "\"2026-W42\"}" }
{ "type": "TOOL_CALL_END",    "toolCallId": "call_1" }
{ "type": "TOOL_CALL_RESULT", "toolCallId": "call_1", "messageId": "msg_2", "content": "{\"already_filed\":0}" }

On screen: a line appears saying “Checking existing expenses…” the moment TOOL_CALL_START arrives, and it flips to a checkmark when the result lands.

A tool call is split into four events for the same reason a message is split into three: the screen can react at each stage instead of waiting for the whole call to finish. The agent is a language model, and it writes the arguments for the tool bit by bit, so they reach us in pieces too.

Each event gives our UI a different moment:

  • TOOL_CALL_START: a tool call has begun, so show its name and a "running" state.
  • TOOL_CALL_ARGS: another fragment of the arguments has arrived, so add it to what we have so far.
  • TOOL_CALL_END: the arguments are complete, so it is now safe to read them.
  • TOOL_CALL_RESULT: here is what the tool returned, so show the result and mark the step done.

One detail catches almost every beginner — the argument fragments are pieces of JSON, and a single piece usually isn’t valid JSON on its own. The first fragment above, {"week":, will make JSON.parse throw an error. The safe rule is to collect the fragments into one string and only parse it after TOOL_CALL_END. If we want to show the arguments live, we can use a tolerant incremental parser, or simply show the tool name until the call is complete.

4. The shared data changes

{
  "type": "STATE_DELTA",
  "delta": [
    { "op": "replace", "path": "/expenses/3/status", "value": "duplicate" }
  ]
}

On screen: the second City Cabs row greys out and gets a “duplicate” tag. Nobody asked for a reload, and the agent didn’t send a new copy of the expense list, it sent one small change.

We might ask why the agent doesn’t just send the whole list again each time. With twelve receipts that would be fine, but real state can be large, and resending it for every tiny change wastes data and makes the screen redraw things that didn’t change, a delta says only what is different.

Each delta is a list of operations, and each operation has three parts:

  • op: what to do. Here it is replace.
  • path: where in the data to do it. Here it points to the status of the item at position 3 in expenses.
  • value: the new value. Here it is "duplicate".

That is why only one row on screen changes. I’ll explain this format properly in a later section, because state sync is where first implementations most often go wrong.

5. The agent flags the dinner

{
  "type": "STATE_DELTA",
  "delta": [
    { "op": "replace", "path": "/expenses/4/status", "value": "needs_approval" }
  ]
}

This is followed by a final message: “One dinner is over the $150 limit. Want me to include it?”

On screen: the Harbour Grill row is highlighted, and an Approve button appears.

Two kinds of events work together here, and each has its own job:

  • STATE_DELTA: changes the data, so the row is marked needs_approval and our UI highlights it and shows the button.
  • TEXT_MESSAGE_*: explains in words why the row is highlighted and what the agent is asking.

Putting the status in the shared data, and not only in the chat text, means our screen doesn’t have to read the sentence to know what to show. It just looks at the status field.

6. The run ends

{ "type": "RUN_FINISHED", "threadId": "thread_42", "runId": "run_7" }

On screen: the working indicator disappears, and the send button comes back. A finished run doesn’t mean the conversation is over. The two IDs show why:

  • threadId: the whole conversation, it stays the same.
  • runId: one pass of the agent. A new one is created for each turn.

When we click Approve, our app starts a new run in the same thread, carrying the answer. The agent sees the earlier messages, knows which expense was waiting, and continues from there. We’ll come back to this when we talk about approvals.

If you want a summary of the vocabulary, there are around sixteen event types, and they fall into five groups:

Memorizing this is not required. The useful part is grouping — If our screen only shows chat text, you can ignore the tool and state groups at first, and add them later.

The mental model that makes it click: a reducer

If you have ever written a frontend with Redux or React’s useReducer, you already know the pattern AG-UI clients follow. A reducer takes the current state and one event, and returns the next state. An AG-UI client is that, with the agent's events as the input.

Here is a stripped-down version in TypeScript. It’s illustrative, and the official client SDK does this bookkeeping for you, but writing it once yourself is the quickest way to understand the protocol:

import { applyPatch } from "fast-json-patch"; // any JSON Patch library works

type Screen = {
  running: boolean;
  messages: Record<string, string>;
  state: any;
};

function reduce(screen: Screen, event: any): Screen {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "RUN_STARTED":
      return { ...screen, running: true };

    case "TEXT_MESSAGE_START":
      return { ...screen, messages: { ...screen.messages, [event.messageId]: "" } };

    case "TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT":
      return {
        ...screen,
        messages: {
          ...screen.messages,
          [event.messageId]: screen.messages[event.messageId] + event.delta,
        },
      };

    case "STATE_DELTA":
      return { ...screen, state: applyPatch(screen.state, event.delta).newDocument };

    case "RUN_FINISHED":
      return { ...screen, running: false };

    default:
      return screen; // events you don't handle yet are safe to ignore
  }
}

That is most of a working client. Events come in, our function turns each one into the next version of the screen’s data, and our UI draws whatever that data says. Run the expense example through it and the whole story plays out: the working indicator switches on at RUN_STARTED, the chat bubble fills in chunk by chunk, the taxi row greys out when a STATE_DELTA arrives, and the indicator switches off at RUN_FINISHED.

The code never asks which agent framework produced the events. It only knows the shape of each event, and that is the point of the protocol. Everything we cover from here (tool calls, state sync, approvals) is just more cases inside the same switch. Once this loop makes sense, the rest of AG-UI is details.

Keeping the screen and the agent in step

State sync is where AG-UI gets its most interesting design decisions, and also where first implementations go wrong. Think about how a text editor saves our work — resaving the entire file after every keystroke would be wasteful. A smarter approach is to save the file once, then record only the edits. AG-UI does the same thing. The agent sends a STATE_SNAPSHOT containing the entire state, then sends STATE_DELTA events containing only what changed.

The deltas use a standard called JSON Patch. It’s a list of operations, each with an op, a path pointing into our JSON, and sometimes a value:

  • replace swaps the value at a path.
  • add inserts something, for example /expenses/- appends to a list.
  • remove deletes the value at a path.
  • move and copy relocate values.

Look back at our delta: "path": "/expenses/3/status" means "inside expenses, take the item at index 3 (the fourth, since counting starts at zero), and change its status." That's the second City Cabs receipt. Because the format is a standard, you don't write the patch logic yourself, since libraries exist for every language.

Sending only changes is cheap, but it has a catch that deserves a careful read. A delta only makes sense if you apply it to the state it was written against. Suppose the connection hiccups and you miss one delta. The next delta still applies cleanly, so no error appears, but our screen is now quietly wrong. It could show the taxi as valid when the agent already removed it, and nothing will tell you.

The protocol specifies how to apply a patch. It does not specify when to stop trusting our copy and ask for a fresh baseline. That judgement is left to us, so teams add their own check. A common one is to compute a hash of the state on both sides every few seconds, compare them, and request a new snapshot if they differ. At the very least, if a patch fails to apply, treat that as a signal to ask for a full snapshot instead of skipping it and moving on.

Three streams on one wire

Our trace was tidy, with one thing happening at a time. In reality, runs aren’t tidy. An agent can type a message while a tool call is in flight and state changes are landing, all interleaved on the same connection.

It helps to think of three logical lanes sharing one physical wire: text messages, tool calls, and state. The events from each lane arrive mixed together, and the IDs (messageId, toolCallId) are what let you sort them back into the right lane.

The number one mistake new developers make is reading the event stream as a strict single sequence, as if each event belongs to whatever came right before it. The moment the agent runs two tools in parallel, that assumption breaks, hence always route by ID.

Mistakes almost everyone can make the first time

This is going to be a short list, because knowing these in advance will save you time.

  • Parsing tool arguments too early — The fragments in TOOL_CALL_ARGS aren't valid JSON until the call ends, so buffer them.
  • Apply a delta to the wrong baseline — If our state object isn’t the one the agent was patching, the patch either fails or silently corrupts our data. Always start from a snapshot and keep every delta in order.
  • Ignore events you don’t recognize by crashing — New event types get added over time, and our default branch should quietly pass them through.
  • Reusing a messageId across different kinds of message — The spec treats an ID as belonging to one kind of message, and mixing a text message with an activity message under the same ID leaves the client with incompatible content shapes and no sensible way to merge them.
  • Assumption that every framework sends every event — This one deserves its own section, but I’ll flag it now: the protocol defines the full list, and our framework’s adapter decides how much of it you actually receive.

Letting a human step in

Let’s go back to the dinner example — A good agent should stop and ask for review and approval, and for anything with real consequences, this is the feature that matters most.

One thing to know before relying on it: AG-UI today has no dedicated “pause and wait for approval” event. We build the pause from the pieces we have, remember the expense run we traced earlier. In step 5 the agent marked the dinner as needs_approval in the shared data and asked about it in a message, and in step 6 the run ended with RUN_FINISHED. That ending is the pause. When the user clicks Approve, our app starts a new run in the same thread, carrying the answer, and the agent picks up from there. Another common pattern is for the agent to propose a tool call such as "submit expenses", have the app intercept it, show a confirmation, and hold the run until the user responds.

Both approaches work, but every team ends up building its own version, which is exactly the sort of duplicated effort a protocol is supposed to remove. So we are proposing a native version. In the draft, a run can finish with an outcome of "interrupt" plus a list of what needs our answer, each with an ID and a reason. Our app renders the question, and our reply starts the next run with a resume list that addresses each interrupt by ID. The new field is optional, so older clients that have never heard of interrupts keep working.

I want to be clear that this is a draft proposal and it may change or be withdrawn, so use it as a preview of where things are heading and not as something to build against.

Where AG-UI sits next to MCP and A2A

We often see three protocol names mentioned together, and they are easy to mix up. Each one covers a different connection in the same system, so here they are for our expense agent.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects an agent to tools and data. When the expense agent asks the expense system what has already been filed, or pulls a receipt from a file store, MCP is the standard way to wire that up. It is how the agent reaches out into the world.

A2A (Agent2Agent) connects one agent to another. Imagine the expense agent handing the “does this dinner break policy?” question to a separate compliance agent built by a different team, possibly on a different framework. A2A is the standard for agents to discover and delegate to each other.

AG-UI connects an agent to the person. Everything we have walked through in this post lives here: progress, shared data, and approvals.

If the agent were a person at a desk, MCP would be their phone and filing cabinet, A2A would be the colleague they call for a second opinion, and AG-UI would be the window where the customer stands and watch.

They aren’t competitors, and a single system can use all three at once. One real difference worth keeping in mind, though — MCP and A2A change what an agent can do, while AG-UI changes what a person can see and control. An agent runs perfectly well without AG-UI, we adopt it because we want a human watching and steering, and that makes it a product decision as much as an architecture one.

Where it stands today

The project is open source under the MIT license and has official TypeScript and Python SDKs. Adoption has been increasing since it was introduced. LangGraph and CrewAI were early partners; Microsoft Agent Framework has an AG-UI integration, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore lists it as a supported protocol next to MCP and A2A, and Pydantic AI has one as well. The integrations page in the AG-UI docs has the current list, and it changes often, so check it for adoption instead of trusting a blog post, including this one.

The spec is also looks constantly getting updated. The docs carry a set of draft proposals that are explicitly marked as under review and subject to change or withdrawal:

  • Interrupt-aware run lifecycle — the native approval flow described above.
  • Reasoning events — a separate stream so a UI can show a model’s reasoning apart from its answer, including a way to carry back encrypted reasoning that the client can’t read.
  • Multi-modal messages — so user messages can carry images, audio, video and documents instead of only text.
  • Generative UI — where an agent proposes a constrained interface for the app to check and display, instead of you hand-building a renderer for every tool.
  • Meta events — for things like thumbs-up feedback and annotations that don’t belong to any particular run.

None of these are final, so don’t build on it yet, though it is worth watching and following, since it shows what the maintainers consider missing from the current version.

What AG-UI does not do

We also need to know the limits to avoid unpleasant behaviours.

  • It doesn’t draw our screen — the protocol tells what is happening, and code that turns it into a card, a progress bar or a button is entirely our responsibility.
  • It doesn’t remember the conversations — requests are stateless, so carrying the message history from one turn to the next is our job.
  • It does not manages permissions — state goes to every connected client by default, and nothing in the protocol says who may see which data or trigger which tool. If our agent retrieves anything sensitive, such as private documents or personal records, it is on our part to filter what reaches each client and check who is allowed to approve what. The same gap means a tool call proposed by a prompt-injected agent looks identical to a legitimate one at the protocol level, so tool whitelisting and confirmation for risky actions need to live in our app.

Framework support is still evolving, hence uneven. Each framework has an adapter that translates its internals into AG-UI events, and those adapters aren’t equally complete. Two frameworks that both advertise AG-UI support can send you different subsets of the event list. Hence before you design your UI around a specific event, check compatibility with framework you are currently using.

Should you use it?

If a person sits at the screen during the run, watching progress or approving actions, then yes. Without AG-UI you would end up inventing a private, less complete version of the same thing, and every new agent you add would need its own glue code.

If our agent runs in the background and someone reviews the result later, think twice. What you probably need there is an audit trail and a review step, and a plain queue with an approval screen may do that with much less machinery than a live event stream.

If you decide to try it, here is the order I’d recommend.

  • Run the quickstart and print every raw event to the console before you build any UI, so you see the real shapes.
  • Write the small reducer from earlier and render only text.
  • Then add tool calls, then shared state, and last of all approvals.

Each step will start making more sense because you did the one before it.

Wrapping up

The expense agent was never the real problem. The problem was the x number of seconds when nobody could see it work, and nobody could say “wait, not that one.” AG-UI gives an agent a standard way to show its work and ask for permission, and gives our app a standard way to listen.

It is young, parts of it are still drafts, and you’ll have to bring you own answers for permissions, history and rendering. Even so, the core idea is sound and simple enough to hold in our head: a stream of small labeled events, a reducer on the client, and a snapshot plus deltas for shared state. If you remember only that, you can read any AG-UI trace and know what’s going on.
